People Who Never Reached Age 50

Thomas Aquinas

Birth date: December 31, 1225

Death date: March 6, 1274

Age: 49

Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar, theologian, philosopher, and one of the defining minds of medieval Scholasticism. He joined Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology, shaped Catholic intellectual tradition, and wrote major works including the Summa Theologiae and Summa contra Gentiles. In 1274, while traveling to the Second Council of Lyon, he became seriously ill after a head injury and was taken to Fossanova Abbey, where Cistercian monks cared for him until his death on 7 March.

James A. Garfield

Birth date: November 18, 1831

Death date: September 18, 1881

Age: 49

James Abram Garfield was the 20th president of the United States, a former Union general, educator, lawyer, preacher, and long-serving congressman from Ohio. Elected in 1880 as a compromise Republican nominee, he is remembered for his intellect, support for civil rights, anti-corruption instincts, and advocacy of civil service reform. Garfield was shot by Charles J. Guiteau on July 2, 1881, only months into his presidency, and died on September 19, 1881, after infections related to the wound.

Douglas Adams

Birth date: March 10, 1952

Death date: May 10, 2001

Age: 49

Douglas Noël Adams was an English author, humorist, screenwriter, and technology enthusiast, best remembered as the creator of The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy and the Dirk Gently novels. His comic imagination mixed science fiction, philosophy, absurdity, and sharp wordplay, making him one of Britain’s most distinctive modern comic writers. Adams died suddenly in Santa Barbara, California, after collapsing from a heart attack while resting from a workout at a gym; he was 49.

John F. Kennedy was the 35th president of the United States, a former U.S. Navy officer, congressman, and senator from Massachusetts whose presidency became closely associated with Cold War crises, the Peace Corps, the space race, and a youthful vision of public service. He was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, on November 22, 1963, while riding in a presidential motorcade, and was pronounced dead shortly afterward at age 46.

Anton Chekhov

Birth date: January 28, 1860

Death date: July 14, 1904

Age: 44

Anton Pavlovich Chekhov was a Russian playwright, short-story writer, and physician whose spare, psychologically subtle style helped reshape modern drama and fiction. His major plays include The Seagull, Uncle Vanya, Three Sisters, and The Cherry Orchard, while his stories remain landmarks of literary realism. Long ill with tuberculosis, he traveled to Badenweiler, Germany, seeking relief; he died there on 15 July 1904 at the age of 44 after years of declining health.

Vincent van Gogh

Birth date: March 29, 1853

Death date: July 28, 1890

Age: 37

Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose bold colour, expressive brushwork and emotional intensity helped shape modern art. Although he worked seriously as an artist for only about a decade, he produced masterpieces including Sunflowers, The Starry Night and many self-portraits. He struggled with mental illness and poverty, and died in Auvers-sur-Oise after shooting himself, passing away two days later at the age of 37.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart

Birth date: January 26, 1756

Death date: December 4, 1791

Age: 35

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer and musician of the Classical period, celebrated for operas, symphonies, concertos, chamber music, and sacred works that helped define Western music. A child prodigy from Salzburg, he later built his mature career in Vienna. He died there on 5 December 1791 at age 35 after a short illness; the exact medical cause remains uncertain, and his Requiem was left unfinished.

Oscar Wilde

Birth date: October 15, 1854

Death date: November 29, 1900

Age: 46

Oscar Wilde was an Irish author, poet, essayist and playwright, celebrated for his dazzling wit, aesthetic style and works such as The Picture of Dorian Gray and The Importance of Being Earnest. A defining literary figure of late Victorian culture, he became famous in London for his comedies, epigrams and flamboyant public persona. After imprisonment and exile, his health declined; he died in Paris on 30 November 1900 from meningitis, commonly linked to an ear infection, at the age of 46.

Martin Luther King Jr.

Birth date: January 14, 1929

Death date: April 3, 1968

Age: 39

Martin Luther King Jr. was an American Baptist minister and civil rights leader whose advocacy of nonviolent resistance made him one of the defining figures of the U.S. civil rights movement. He helped lead the Montgomery bus boycott, co-founded the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, delivered the landmark “I Have a Dream” speech, and received the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize. In his final years, he broadened his work to address poverty and opposition to the Vietnam War. King was assassinated on April 4, 1968, in Memphis, Tennessee, while supporting striking sanitation workers and preparing the Poor People’s Campaign. He died at the age of 39.

George Orwell

Birth date: June 24, 1903

Death date: January 20, 1950

Age: 46

George Orwell, born Eric Arthur Blair, was an English novelist, essayist, journalist, and critic whose clear prose and fierce opposition to totalitarianism made him one of the defining political writers of the twentieth century. He is best remembered for Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, works that turned terms like Big Brother and Orwellian into lasting cultural shorthand. His final years were marked by severe tuberculosis; after completing Nineteen Eighty-Four, he was treated in hospital in London, where he died from the disease on 21 January 1950 at the age of 46.

Franz Kafka

Birth date: July 2, 1883

Death date: June 2, 1924

Age: 40

Franz Kafka was a Prague-born German-language Jewish writer whose fiction transformed modern literature with visions of alienation, absurd bureaucracy, guilt, anxiety, and fragile identity. His best-known works include The Metamorphosis, The Trial, and The Castle, many of which became famous only after his friend Max Brod ignored Kafka’s request to destroy unpublished manuscripts. He died in 1924 at a sanatorium near Vienna after tuberculosis, especially affecting his throat, made eating extremely painful; he was 40 years old.

Qin Shi Huang

Birth date: January 31, 259 BCE

Death date: July 11, 210 BCE

Age: 49
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Qin Shi Huang was an authoritarian imperial ruler whose legacy includes wars of conquest, harsh Legalist punishments, forced labor on enormous state projects, censorship, and traditional accounts of book burning and executions of scholars. Some details of those accounts are debated, but his rule is strongly associated with coercive centralized power.

Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, was the founder of the Qin dynasty and the first emperor of a unified China. After defeating the rival Warring States, he centralized rule, standardized writing, weights, measures and coinage, expanded roads and walls, and left behind the famous mausoleum guarded by the Terracotta Army. He died in 210 BC during his fifth inspection tour of eastern China after becoming seriously ill; later tradition links his final years to an obsession with immortality, and mercury-based elixirs have often been suggested as a possible factor, though the exact cause remains uncertain.

Albert Camus

Birth date: November 6, 1913

Death date: January 3, 1960

Age: 46

Albert Camus was a French-Algerian writer, philosopher, journalist, playwright, and one of the defining literary voices of the twentieth century. Born in French Algeria, he became famous for works such as The Stranger, The Plague, The Myth of Sisyphus, The Fall, and The Rebel, and received the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature. His writing explored absurdity, revolt, moral responsibility, and human dignity in a violent century. Camus died on 4 January 1960 at age 46 in a car crash near Sens, France, while traveling in a Facel Vega driven by his friend and publisher Michel Gallimard.

Birth date: June 5, 1799

Death date: February 9, 1837

Age: 37

Alexander Sergeyevich Pushkin was a Russian poet, playwright, and novelist, widely regarded as Russia’s greatest poet and a founder of modern Russian literature. His works, including Eugene Onegin, Boris Godunov, and Ruslan and Ludmila, shaped the literary language of 19th-century Russia. He died in Saint Petersburg at 37 after being fatally wounded in a duel with Georges d’Anthès, a French officer linked to rumors around Pushkin’s wife.

Frida Kahlo was a Mexican painter celebrated for vivid self-portraits and works rooted in Mexican folk culture, identity, gender, pain, and political life. Her art blended realism, symbolism, and fantasy, making her one of the most recognizable artists of the twentieth century. She lived with lasting health problems after childhood polio and a severe bus accident, and died in 1954 at age 47. The official cause of death was pulmonary embolism, though no autopsy was performed and some later accounts have questioned the exact circumstances.

Birth date: July 19, 357 BCE

Death date: June 9, 324 BCE

Age: 32

Alexander the Great, king of Macedon and one of antiquity’s most influential commanders, inherited the throne at 20 and built an empire stretching from Greece through Egypt and Persia toward northwestern India. Undefeated in battle, he spread Greek political and cultural influence across much of the ancient world. He died in Babylon in June 323 BCE after a sudden illness, before securing a clear succession, leaving his empire to fragment among his generals. He was 32.

Edgar Allan Poe was an American writer, poet, editor, and critic whose tales of mystery and the macabre helped define Gothic fiction and the modern detective story. Best known for works such as "The Raven" and his short fiction, he became one of the most influential figures in early American literature. He died in Baltimore on October 7, 1849, aged 40, after being found in a distressed and confused condition; the exact cause of death remains unknown.

Birth date: January 7, 1935

Death date: August 15, 1977

Age: 42

Elvis Aaron Presley was an American singer and actor known worldwide as the “King of Rock and Roll.” Born in Tupelo, Mississippi and raised in Memphis, he helped transform popular music in the 1950s with a powerful mix of rockabilly, rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and charismatic stage presence. His recordings, films, television appearances, and Las Vegas performances made him one of the most influential entertainers of the 20th century. Presley died at his Graceland estate in Memphis on August 16, 1977, after years of declining health linked to prescription drug use and other medical issues. He was 42.

Marilyn Monroe, born Norma Jeane Mortenson, was an American actress and model who became one of Hollywood’s defining icons of the 1950s. Famous for films such as Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, The Seven Year Itch, and Some Like It Hot, she combined comic timing, glamour, and vulnerability in a way that made her a lasting pop-culture figure. She died at age 36 at her Los Angeles home from a barbiturate overdose, and her death was ruled a probable suicide.

Che Guevara

Birth date: June 13, 1928

Death date: October 8, 1967

Age: 39
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Che Guevara is highly polarizing because he was a Marxist revolutionary and guerrilla leader associated with armed insurgency, political violence, revolutionary executions, and support for authoritarian communist rule in Cuba. Admirers view him as an anti-imperialist symbol, while critics emphasize repression, killings, and ideological extremism.

Ernesto “Che” Guevara was an Argentine Marxist revolutionary, physician, author, guerrilla leader, diplomat, and a central figure in the Cuban Revolution. He became one of the 20th century’s most recognizable political icons, associated with anti-imperialism, guerrilla warfare, and revolutionary internationalism. After leaving Cuba to promote revolutions abroad, he fought in Bolivia, where he was captured by Bolivian forces and executed on 9 October 1967 at the age of 39.

Rosa Luxemburg

Birth date: March 4, 1871

Death date: January 14, 1919

Age: 47

Rosa Luxemburg was a Polish-born, naturalised-German Marxist theorist, economist, writer, and revolutionary socialist. A major figure in the Social Democratic Party of Germany and later a co-founder of the Spartacus League and the Communist Party of Germany, she became known for her sharp critiques of reformism, imperialism, militarism, and authoritarian socialism. During the German Revolution, she was captured after the failed Spartacist uprising in Berlin and murdered on 15 January 1919 by Freikorps soldiers; she was 47.

Sung Jae-gi was a South Korean activist and writer known for leading Man of Korea and other masculinist, anti-feminist organizations, while also running support efforts for vulnerable men. A polarizing public figure, he campaigned against what he saw as reverse discrimination. In July 2013, amid heavy debts connected to his organization, he announced a dramatic bridge-jump appeal for donations and jumped from Seoul’s Mapo Bridge into the Han River; his body was found days later.

Jane Austen

Birth date: December 15, 1775

Death date: July 17, 1817

Age: 41

Jane Austen was an English novelist whose sharply observant fiction transformed the novel of manners and helped shape literary realism. Best known for Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility, Emma, Mansfield Park, Persuasion, and Northanger Abbey, she wrote with wit, irony, and unusual insight into class, marriage, money, and women’s limited choices in Georgian society. Her fame grew greatly after her death, and her books have remained central to English literature. In her final year she suffered a serious, poorly understood illness, moved to Winchester to seek medical help, and died there on 18 July 1817 at the age of 41; later theories have included Addison’s disease, Hodgkin lymphoma, lupus, tuberculosis, and cancer.

Simón Bolívar

Birth date: July 23, 1783

Death date: December 16, 1830

Age: 47

Simón Bolívar was a Venezuelan military and political leader known as El Libertador for his central role in the independence of Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Peru, and Venezuela from Spanish rule. A visionary but often controversial statesman, he tried to unite parts of South America under Gran Colombia and became a lasting symbol of Latin American independence. In his final months, exhausted, politically isolated, and ill, he withdrew toward the Caribbean coast and died near Santa Marta on 17 December 1830, officially reported as tuberculosis, at the age of 47.

Birth date: November 9, 1759

Death date: May 8, 1805

Age: 45

Friedrich Schiller was a major German playwright, poet, philosopher, and historian, central to Weimar Classicism and remembered for works such as The Robbers, Don Carlos, William Tell, and Ode to Joy. A close collaborator and friend of Goethe, he helped shape modern German literature and dramatic thought. Schiller’s final years were marked by serious chronic illness, especially lung disease often described as tuberculosis. He died in Weimar on 9 May 1805 at the age of 45, while still creatively active.

Birth date: April 8, 1821

Death date: August 30, 1867

Age: 46

Charles Baudelaire was a French poet, essayist, translator, and art critic whose Les Fleurs du mal helped reshape modern poetry with its urban intensity, musical language, and unsettling beauty. A major influence on Symbolism and literary modernism, he also translated Edgar Allan Poe and wrote sharply about art and modern life. His final years were marked by debt, illness, and collapse: after a massive stroke in 1866, he suffered paralysis and aphasia, spent time in care in Brussels and Paris, and died in Paris on 31 August 1867 at the age of 46.

Lord Byron, born George Gordon Byron, was a British Romantic poet, peer, satirist, and one of the most magnetic literary celebrities of the early nineteenth century. His works, including Childe Harold's Pilgrimage and Don Juan, helped define the restless, defiant Byronic hero. In his final years he supported the Greek struggle for independence against the Ottoman Empire. He died in Missolonghi, Greece, after fever and illness, at the age of 36.

Freddie Mercury

Birth date: September 4, 1946

Death date: November 23, 1991

Age: 45

Freddie Mercury, born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar, was the electrifying lead vocalist and pianist of Queen, celebrated for his four-octave voice, theatrical stagecraft, and classics such as “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Somebody to Love,” and “We Are the Champions.” He helped turn Queen into one of rock’s most iconic bands, with his 1985 Live Aid performance remaining legendary. Diagnosed with AIDS in the late 1980s, he kept working in the studio almost until the end. He publicly confirmed his illness only one day before dying at his Kensington home from AIDS-related bronchial pneumonia at age 45.

Frédéric Chopin was a Polish composer and virtuoso pianist of the Romantic era, celebrated for transforming piano music through his nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises, études, preludes, and ballades. Born near Warsaw and later based in Paris, he became one of music’s earliest international celebrities while writing with a deeply personal, poetic style. Long troubled by poor health, he died in Paris on 17 October 1849 at the age of 39, most commonly attributed to tuberculosis, with later medical discussion suggesting complications involving tuberculous pericarditis.

James Clerk Maxwell

Birth date: June 12, 1831

Death date: November 4, 1879

Age: 48

James Clerk Maxwell was a Scottish physicist and mathematician whose work unified electricity, magnetism, and light through the classical theory of electromagnetic radiation. His equations became one of the foundations of modern physics, and he also made major contributions to statistical mechanics, color theory, optics, and control theory. In 1871 he became the first Cavendish Professor of Physics at Cambridge. Maxwell died in Cambridge on 5 November 1879, aged 48, after suffering from abdominal or stomach cancer.

Benedictus de Spinoza

Birth date: November 23, 1632

Death date: February 20, 1677

Age: 44

Baruch Spinoza, also known by his Latin name Benedictus de Spinoza, was a Portuguese-Dutch philosopher whose radical rationalism helped shape modern biblical criticism, Enlightenment thought, democratic political theory, and debates about God, nature, freedom, and the mind. Excommunicated from Amsterdam’s Portuguese-Jewish community in 1656, he lived independently as a thinker and lens grinder while writing works such as the Theological-Political Treatise and Ethics. He died in The Hague on 21 February 1677 at age 44, probably from a lung illness often linked to tuberculosis and possibly aggravated by glass dust from lens grinding.

Alan Turing

Birth date: June 22, 1912

Death date: June 6, 1954

Age: 41

Alan Mathison Turing was an English mathematician, logician, cryptanalyst and pioneering computer scientist whose work shaped theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence and modern computing. During the Second World War he played a crucial role at Bletchley Park in breaking German ciphers, including Enigma-related naval traffic. After the war he designed early stored-program computer concepts and explored mathematical biology. In 1952 he was prosecuted for homosexual acts and underwent hormone treatment instead of imprisonment. He died in Wilmslow, Cheshire, on 7 June 1954 from cyanide poisoning; the inquest ruled suicide, though later discussion has noted that accidental poisoning cannot be entirely excluded.

Kahlil Gibran was a Lebanese-American writer, poet, visual artist, and major figure of modern Arabic and English-language literature, best remembered for The Prophet, a 1923 work whose aphoristic spiritual prose reached readers around the world. Born in Bsharri and later active in Boston, Paris, and New York, he blended romanticism, mysticism, symbolism, and immigrant experience into a distinctive literary voice. He died in New York City on April 10, 1931, at age 48; contemporary accounts report cirrhosis of the liver, with incipient tuberculosis also noted.

Death date: August 18, 1662

Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer whose work shaped projective geometry, probability theory, fluid mechanics, and religious philosophy. A prodigy from childhood, he designed early calculating machines and later wrote the influential Lettres provinciales and Pensées. After years of fragile health, his illness worsened sharply in 1662; he suffered convulsions in Paris, received last rites, and died the next morning at age 39.

Birth date: June 28, 1900

Death date: July 30, 1944

Age: 44

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry was a French aviator, writer, poet and journalist whose flying career shaped some of the most memorable literature of the 20th century. He worked on pioneering airmail routes across Europe, Africa and South America, and his books, including Night Flight, Wind, Sand and Stars and The Little Prince, combined adventure, moral reflection and poetic clarity. During World War II he flew reconnaissance missions for France. On 31 July 1944, aged 44, his aircraft disappeared over the Mediterranean during a mission near Corsica and Marseille; wreckage was later found, but the exact cause of the crash remains uncertain.

He died in New York City on 8 December 1980 after being shot outside the Dakota apartment building, shortly after returning from a recording session.

Mehmed II, known as Mehmed the Conqueror, was the Ottoman sultan whose capture of Constantinople in 1453 ended the Byzantine Empire and transformed the city into the empire’s great capital. A brilliant and ambitious ruler, he expanded Ottoman power across Anatolia and the Balkans while strengthening law, administration, architecture, and learning. In 1481, while setting out on another campaign, he became gravely ill near Gebze; gout was reported, and later accounts raised the possibility of poisoning. He died aged 49.

He died suddenly in Hong Kong on 1973-07-20 at the age of 32 after collapsing into a coma; cerebral edema is commonly cited, while the exact cause remains debated.

Heinrich Himmler was a German Nazi politician and military leader, best known as Reichsführer-SS and one of the most powerful figures in Nazi Germany. He built the SS into a vast instrument of terror, controlled major police and security forces, and played a central role in organizing the Holocaust and Nazi occupation policies. In the final weeks of World War II, after failed attempts to negotiate with the Western Allies, he was dismissed by Hitler, captured by British forces, and died by suicide in custody on 23 May 1945 at the age of 44.

Swami Vivekananda, born Narendranath Datta, was an Indian Hindu monk, philosopher, author, and the leading disciple of Ramakrishna. He became one of the most influential modern interpreters of Vedanta and Yoga, gaining international fame after his 1893 address at the World’s Parliament of Religions in Chicago. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission and helped shape modern Hindu thought and Indian nationalism. After years of intense travel, teaching, and declining health, he died quietly at Belur Math on 4 July 1902, reportedly while meditating; a cerebral blood vessel rupture has been suggested as a possible cause.

Babur, born Zahir-ud-Din Muhammad, was a Timurid prince, poet, memoirist, and military leader who founded the Mughal Empire after defeating Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526. He died in Agra on 26 December 1530, aged 47, and was succeeded by his son Humayun; his remains were later moved to Kabul in accordance with his wishes.

Paracelsus, born Theophrastus von Hohenheim, was a Swiss-German physician, alchemist, philosopher and medical reformer of the Renaissance. In 1541 he moved to Salzburg, where he died on 24 September at the age of 47 and was buried at St. Sebastian’s cemetery; later stories claimed poisoning or violence, but the exact circumstances remain uncertain.

Alexander III of Russia was Emperor of Russia, King of Poland, and Grand Duke of Finland from 1881 until 1894. A firm autocrat, he reversed many of Alexander II’s liberal reforms, promoted Russian nationalism, and became known as “the Peacemaker” because Russia fought no major wars during his reign. His later years were marked by declining health, and in 1894 he became gravely ill with kidney disease. Too weak to travel farther, he remained at Livadia in Crimea, where he died on 1 November 1894 at the age of 49.

John, King of England from 1199 to 1216, was the youngest son of Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine and is remembered as John Lackland. His reign saw the loss of Normandy to Philip II of France, conflict with the papacy, heavy taxation, and the baronial crisis that led to the sealing of Magna Carta in 1215. Maximilien Robespierre was a French lawyer, Jacobin politician, and one of the most influential figures of the French Revolution. He championed political equality, universal male suffrage, civic virtue, and the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade, while becoming closely associated with the Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror. In July 1794, amid rising fear of his power and policies, he was overthrown in the Thermidorian Reaction, arrested, and guillotined in Paris without trial at the age of 36.

He spent much of his life as a teacher, writer, and translator in Berlin, often in financial difficulty. In 1856, still obscure and poor, he developed a severe fever or tumor reportedly following an insect bite or sting on the neck. He died in Berlin at age 49, with only a small circle aware of his passing.

Selim I, known as Yavuz Sultan Selim or Selim the Grim, was the Ottoman sultan from 1512 to 1520. In only eight years he dramatically expanded Ottoman power, defeating the Safavids at Chaldiran and conquering the Mamluk Sultanate, bringing Syria, Egypt, the Hejaz, and key pilgrimage routes under Ottoman control. He died near Çorlu after a severe illness, traditionally linked to a badly treated carbuncle or boil, though later writers have suggested other causes such as cancer or plague.

Mary I, often called Mary Tudor, was Queen of England and Ireland from 1553 to 1558 and the first queen regnant of England. Nero was the fifth Roman emperor and the last ruler of the Julio-Claudian dynasty, reigning from AD 54 to 68. Remembered for his theatrical tastes, ambitious building projects, political violence, and the controversies surrounding the Great Fire of Rome, he remains one of antiquity’s most notorious rulers. Facing rebellion, abandonment by key supporters, and condemnation by the Senate, Nero fled Rome and died by suicide on 9 June AD 68 at the age of 30.

Giacomo Leopardi

Birth date: June 28, 1798

Death date: June 13, 1837

Age: 38

Giacomo Leopardi was one of Italy’s greatest nineteenth-century poets and thinkers, admired for the Canti, the Operette morali, and the vast Zibaldone. His writing fused lyric beauty, classical learning, and a severe meditation on desire, nature, suffering, and human illusion. Frail for much of his life, he spent his last years in Naples with Antonio Ranieri. He died there suddenly at 38 during the 1837 cholera epidemic; the immediate cause is often described as pulmonary edema, heart failure, or dropsy, and Ranieri helped prevent his burial in a common epidemic grave.

Joseph II, Holy Roman Emperor

Birth date: March 12, 1741

Death date: February 19, 1790

Age: 48

Joseph II was Holy Roman Emperor from 1765 and sole ruler of the Habsburg Monarchy from 1780, remembered as one of Europe’s most energetic enlightened absolutists. He pushed reforms in religion, law, education, administration, serfdom, and state centralization, often faster than his empire could absorb. His final years were clouded by war, resistance in Hungary and the Austrian Netherlands, and the rollback of several reforms. Already seriously ill after returning to Vienna, he suffered worsening fever, coughing, breathing problems, and chest pain, probably linked to pulmonary tuberculosis, and died in Vienna at age 48.

Francis Xavier

Birth date: April 6, 1506

Death date: December 2, 1552

Age: 46

Francis Xavier was a Navarrese Catholic cleric, missionary, and co-founder of the Society of Jesus. A close companion of Ignatius of Loyola, he became one of the most influential Christian missionaries of the early modern era, working across India, Southeast Asia, and Japan and helping launch the first major Christian mission to Japan. In 1552 he tried to enter Ming China but was stranded on Shangchuan Island, where he fell ill while waiting for passage to the mainland. He died there on 3 December 1552 at the age of 46.

Death date: August 1, 1921

Age: 48

Enrico Caruso was an Italian operatic tenor from Naples whose powerful, warm voice made him one of the defining singers of the early 20th century. He became a star at leading opera houses in Europe and the Americas, especially the Metropolitan Opera, and was one of the first global celebrities created by commercial recordings. After serious health problems in his final year, he died in Naples on 2 August 1921, with his death commonly attributed to peritonitis, linked in some accounts to a subphrenic abscess and pneumonia.

Death date: February 7, 1849

Age: 48

France Prešeren was Slovenia’s great Romantic poet and a lawyer, remembered for transforming Slovene into a powerful literary language and for works such as “A Wreath of Sonnets” and “Zdravljica,” later connected with Slovenia’s national anthem. His poetry fused personal longing, patriotic feeling, and European Romantic form. In his final years he worked in Kranj, where worsening liver disease, commonly identified as cirrhosis, confined him to bed before his death on 8 February 1849 at age 48.

Vlad III, better known as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula, was a 15th-century voivode of Wallachia whose campaigns against Ottoman power and severe punishments made him one of medieval Europe’s most infamous rulers. After briefly regaining power in 1476, he was killed near Bucharest or Snagov while fighting Ottoman-backed forces; accounts say his head was sent to the sultan.

Death date: December 18, 1848

Age: 30

Emily Jane Brontë was an English novelist and poet, best remembered for her only novel, Wuthering Heights, a fierce and atmospheric classic of English literature published under the pen name Ellis Bell. Raised in the Yorkshire village of Haworth with her literary siblings Charlotte and Anne, she lived a largely private life shaped by the moors, family imagination, and intense creative discipline. Her health declined rapidly in 1848, soon after the death of her brother Branwell; she refused medical help until it was too late and died of tuberculosis in Haworth at the age of 30.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Titus is controversial because, before becoming emperor, he commanded Roman forces in the Jewish War and captured Jerusalem in 70 CE. That campaign involved mass death, enslavement, and the destruction of the Second Temple, one of the most traumatic events in Jewish history.

Titus Flavius Vespasianus was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 CE and a leading figure of the Flavian dynasty. Before ruling, he commanded Roman forces in the Jewish War and captured Jerusalem in 70, an event later commemorated by the Arch of Titus. As emperor he completed the Colosseum and became known for disaster relief after Vesuvius and a major fire in Rome. His reign was brief: after the amphitheatre games, he fell ill and died of fever on 13 September 81, aged 41, and was succeeded by his brother Domitian.

Death date: April 15, 1958

Age: 37

Rosalind Franklin was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer whose precise experimental work helped reveal the molecular structures of DNA, RNA, viruses, coal, and graphite. Her DNA research at King’s College London, especially the evidence connected with Photo 51, became central to the discovery of the double helix. She died in London of ovarian cancer on 16 April 1958, aged 37, before the Nobel Prize recognition given to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins in 1962.

Anders Celsius was a Swedish astronomer, physicist and mathematician, best remembered for proposing the centigrade temperature scale that later took his name. He died in Uppsala from tuberculosis in 1744, only 42 years old, before the Celsius scale was reversed into its modern form.

Robert Francis Kennedy was an American lawyer and Democratic politician, best known as U.S. attorney general under his brother President John F. Kennedy and later as a U.S. senator from New York. Alexander Alexandrovich Blok was one of the defining Russian poets of the Silver Age and a leading voice of Russian Symbolism, remembered for his musical lyricism, mystical imagery, and revolutionary-era poem The Twelve. Born in Saint Petersburg into an intellectual family, he became a central literary figure of early twentieth-century Russia. He died in Petrograd on 7 August 1921 at age 40, after severe physical decline; sources describe heart failure brought on by malnutrition and the exhaustion of the post-revolutionary years.

Why this is controversial: Felix Dzerzhinsky is extremely controversial as the founder and first head of the Cheka, the Soviet political police. Felix Dzerzhinsky was a Polish-born Bolshevik revolutionary and Soviet politician, best known as the founder and first leader of the Cheka, the Soviet state security organization that later evolved through the GPU and OGPU. Nicknamed “Iron Felix,” he became one of the most feared and symbolic figures of early Soviet power, closely associated with the Red Terror and the creation of a repressive security apparatus. He died in Moscow on 20 July 1926 after suffering a heart attack, reportedly shortly after delivering a forceful speech to the Bolshevik Central Committee.

Death date: June 26, 1844

Age: 38
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Joseph Smith is a deeply contested religious and political founder. Controversies include the origins and truth claims of the Book of Mormon, plural marriage, theocratic power in Nauvoo, conflict with critics, destruction of an opposition press, and the enduring divide between believers' and critics' accounts of his life.

Joseph Smith Jr. was an American religious and political leader best known as the founder of Mormonism and the Latter Day Saint movement. He published the Book of Mormon in 1830 and organized a church that later developed into several denominations, including the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. His teachings, revelations, and leadership attracted many followers but also intense opposition. In 1844, after conflict in Nauvoo, Illinois, Smith was jailed in Carthage and was shot and killed by a mob at the age of 38.

Death date: January 14, 1919

Age: 47

Karl Liebknecht was a German socialist politician, lawyer, and revolutionary, best known as a fierce opponent of World War I and as a co-founder of the Spartacus League and the Communist Party of Germany alongside Rosa Luxemburg. A member of the Reichstag, he became famous for rejecting the political consensus behind Germany’s war effort. In January 1919, after the failed Spartacist uprising in Berlin, he was captured by Freikorps troops and summarily killed, becoming a lasting martyr of the German left.

Age: 41
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Shaka Zulu is controversial because his state-building and military reforms are associated with conquest, harsh discipline, executions, and regional upheaval. At the same time, many accounts of his brutality were shaped by hostile or colonial-era sources, so the historical picture is debated.

Shaka kaSenzangakhona, widely known as Shaka Zulu, was the powerful founder and king of the Zulu Kingdom, remembered for reshaping military organization, discipline, and regional politics in southern Africa. His reign from about 1816 to 1828 helped turn the Zulu from a smaller chiefdom into a major force. He was assassinated at KwaDukuza by his half-brothers Dingane and Mhlangana, with Mbopa also traditionally named among the conspirators, after mounting tensions in the royal court.

Murad III was the 12th sultan of the Ottoman Empire, ruling from 1574 to 1595. He died at Topkapı Palace in Constantinople on 16 January 1595, apparently after illness or natural causes, before being buried near Hagia Sophia.

In 1314 he suffered a stroke during a hunt near Pont-Sainte-Maxence and died a few weeks later at Fontainebleau, aged 46.

Billie Holiday, born Eleanora Fagan and nicknamed “Lady Day,” was one of the most influential American jazz and swing singers of the twentieth century. Guillaume Apollinaire was a Polish-French poet, playwright, novelist, journalist, and art critic who helped shape the avant-garde culture of early twentieth-century Paris. Ancient sources portray him as cruel, arbitrary, sexually abusive, financially exploitative, and willing to use executions and humiliation to consolidate personal power. Caligula, born Gaius Julius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, was the third Roman emperor, ruling from 37 to 41 CE; remembered for his volatile reputation, concentration of imperial power, and ambitious public works, he remains one of antiquity’s most debated rulers. In January 41 he was assassinated at the Palatine Games in a conspiracy led by Praetorian officers, ending his reign at age 28.

Death date: September 3, 2006

Age: 44

Steve Irwin was an Australian conservationist, zookeeper, wildlife educator, and television personality whose boundless energy made him internationally famous as the Crocodile Hunter. Through his documentaries, Australia Zoo, and hands-on approach to reptiles and endangered wildlife, he became one of the most recognizable advocates for animal conservation. He died at age 44 on 4 September 2006 while filming an underwater documentary at the Great Barrier Reef, after a stingray barb pierced his chest, causing fatal injury.

Maryam Mirzakhani

Birth date: May 11, 1977

Death date: July 13, 2017

Age: 40

Maryam Mirzakhani was an Iranian mathematician whose work transformed the study of Riemann surfaces, moduli spaces, hyperbolic geometry, and dynamical systems. A professor at Stanford University, she became the first woman and the first Iranian to receive the Fields Medal in 2014. She died at age 40 on 14 July 2017 at Stanford Hospital after breast cancer, first diagnosed in 2013, spread to her liver and bones.

Kurt Cobain

Birth date: February 19, 1967

Death date: April 4, 1994

Age: 27

Kurt Cobain was an American musician, singer, guitarist and songwriter who led Nirvana and helped bring grunge and alternative rock into the global mainstream with songs such as "Smells Like Teen Spirit," "Come as You Are" and "Heart-Shaped Box." A defining voice of early-1990s rock, he was found dead at his Seattle home in April 1994; authorities concluded he died around April 5 from a self-inflicted shotgun wound, aged 27.

Tupac Shakur

Birth date: June 15, 1971

Death date: September 12, 1996

Age: 25

Tupac Shakur was an American rapper, actor, and activist whose intense delivery, political themes, and emotional range made him one of the most influential artists in hip-hop. Known as 2Pac and Makaveli, he helped define 1990s rap with landmark albums, major hit singles, and film roles. He died at 25 on September 13, 1996, six days after being shot in a drive-by attack in Las Vegas, a killing that became one of music history's most notorious cases.

Emiliano Zapata

Birth date: August 7, 1879

Death date: April 9, 1919

Age: 39

Emiliano Zapata Salazar was a Mexican revolutionary, guerrilla leader, and one of the central figures of the Mexican Revolution. As the leading voice of the peasant movement in Morelos, he became closely associated with agrarian reform, the Plan de Ayala, and the demand that land be returned to rural communities. His legacy helped inspire later Zapatismo and made him an enduring symbol of social justice in Mexico. Zapata died at age 39 on 10 April 1919, when he was lured into an ambush at Chinameca, Morelos, and assassinated by forces linked to Venustiano Carranza.

Sofia Kovalevskaya

Birth date: January 14, 1850

Death date: February 9, 1891

Age: 41

Sofya Kovalevskaya was a Russian mathematician and writer whose work in analysis, partial differential equations, and mechanics made her one of the most important scientists of the nineteenth century. She became the first woman in modern Europe to receive a doctorate in mathematics and later held a professorship in Stockholm, breaking barriers in a field that had almost entirely excluded women. She died in Stockholm on 10 February 1891, aged 41, after influenza developed into pneumonia following a trip to Nice.

Catullus

Birth date: December 31, 84 BCE

Death date: December 31, 54 BCE

Age: 30

Gaius Valerius Catullus was one of the sharpest and most personal poets of the late Roman Republic, famous for intense love poems, polished insults, and the emotionally charged figure of Lesbia. Born in Verona and active in Rome, he helped define the neoteric style of Latin poetry. He died young in Rome around 54 BCE, probably at about 30; no reliable ancient account records the medical cause or precise circumstances of his death.

Ayrton Senna

Birth date: March 20, 1960

Death date: April 30, 1994

Age: 34

Ayrton Senna da Silva was a Brazilian Formula One driver, celebrated for his extraordinary speed, wet-weather mastery, fierce competitiveness, and three World Drivers' Championships with McLaren in 1988, 1990, and 1991. He won 41 Grands Prix and became a national hero in Brazil as well as one of motorsport’s most admired figures. Senna died at age 34 on 1 May 1994 after crashing while leading the San Marino Grand Prix at Imola, a tragedy that profoundly changed Formula One safety standards.

Georges Bizet

Death date: June 2, 1875

Age: 36

Georges Bizet was a French Romantic-era composer whose vivid theatrical instinct and gift for melody made him one of the defining voices of 19th-century opera. Although many of his works struggled during his lifetime, his final opera, Carmen, became one of the most frequently performed works in the repertory. He died in Bougival on 3 June 1875, only three months after Carmen’s premiere, reportedly from a heart attack, at the age of 36.

Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky

Birth date: March 20, 1839

Death date: March 27, 1881

Age: 42

Modest Petrovich Mussorgsky was a Russian Romantic composer and a member of The Five, the circle that sought a distinctly Russian musical voice. He is best remembered for Boris Godunov, Night on Bald Mountain, and Pictures at an Exhibition, works admired for their bold realism, dramatic instinct, and national color. His later life was marked by poverty, unfinished projects, heavy drinking, seizures, and delirium tremens; he died in Saint Petersburg shortly after his 42nd birthday, with sources linking his final collapse to alcoholism and heart failure.

Mikhail Yuryevich Lermontov was a major Russian Romantic poet, novelist, playwright, painter, and army officer whose works, especially A Hero of Our Time and his lyric poetry, helped shape modern Russian literature. Exiled to the Caucasus after the poem Death of the Poet made him famous, he later died in 1841 at age 26 after being shot in a duel with fellow officer Nikolai Martynov.

Birth date: April 29, 1883

Death date: January 2, 1923

Age: 39

Jaroslav Hašek was a Czech writer, journalist, humorist and satirist, celebrated above all for the unfinished anti-war masterpiece The Fateful Adventures of the Good Soldier Švejk. A restless bohemian with anarchist and later communist ties, he turned bureaucracy, military discipline and imperial authority into enduring comedy. In his last years he lived in Lipnice nad Sázavou, seriously ill and overweight, dictating parts of Švejk from bed before dying there on 3 January 1923, aged 39, commonly reported from heart disease or heart failure, with some accounts mentioning pneumonia.

Mata Hari

Birth date: August 6, 1876

Death date: October 14, 1917

Age: 41

Mata Hari, born Margaretha Geertruida Zelle in the Netherlands, became one of early twentieth-century Europe’s most famous exotic dancers and courtesans, cultivating a dramatic stage persona that fascinated Parisian society. During World War I, her travels and relationships with officers drew suspicion, and she was convicted by France of spying for Germany. Her guilt remains debated, but she was executed by firing squad at Vincennes on 15 October 1917, aged 41.

Lorenzo de' Medici

Birth date: December 31, 1449

Death date: April 7, 1492

Age: 43

Lorenzo de' Medici, known as Lorenzo the Magnificent, was the de facto ruler of Florence and one of the defining patrons of the Italian Renaissance. He supported artists, poets, philosophers, and political alliances that helped make Florence a cultural capital. His circle is associated with figures such as Botticelli and the young Michelangelo. In his final years, Florence faced financial strain and religious agitation under Savonarola's influence. Lorenzo died at the Medici villa at Careggi in April 1492, reportedly after a peaceful deathbed scene, at the age of 43.

Oliver Goldsmith

Birth date: November 9, 1728

Death date: April 3, 1774

Age: 45

Oliver Goldsmith was an Anglo-Irish poet, novelist, playwright, essayist, and hack writer of the Georgian era, admired for the novel The Vicar of Wakefield, the poem The Deserted Village, and the comedy She Stoops to Conquer. A friend of Samuel Johnson and Sir Joshua Reynolds, he became a memorable figure in London literary society despite chronic debt and ill health. He died in London on 4 April 1774, probably after a severe illness connected with kidney trouble and ill-advised self-treatment, and was buried at Temple Church. He was 45.

Death date: December 31, 297 BCE

Age: 43

Chandragupta Maurya was the founder and first emperor of the Maurya Empire, remembered for overthrowing the Nanda dynasty, unifying much of the Indian subcontinent, and building an imperial administration associated with his adviser Chanakya. His reign helped shape one of ancient India’s most powerful states. Late Jain tradition says he abdicated, became an ascetic at Shravanabelagola, and died by ritual fasting, making his estimated age at death 43.

Srinivasa Ramanujan

Birth date: December 21, 1887

Death date: April 25, 1920

Age: 32

Srinivasa Ramanujan was an Indian mathematician whose extraordinary intuition transformed number theory, infinite series, continued fractions, partitions, and modular forms. Largely self-taught, he developed thousands of identities and formulas, many later proved correct and influential. His correspondence with G. H. Hardy brought him to Cambridge, where his originality astonished leading mathematicians. In 1919, worsening illness forced him to return to India; he died in Kumbakonam on 26 April 1920, aged 32, while still producing new mathematical ideas.

Death date: April 1, 670

Age: 45

Hasan ibn Ali was the eldest son of Ali and Fatima, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, and a major early Islamic political and religious leader. Recognized as the second Imam in Shia Islam, he briefly ruled as caliph in 661 before making a peace treaty with Mu'awiya and withdrawing to Medina. He died there in 670 at about 45; many early accounts say he was poisoned, often naming his wife Ja'da bint al-Ash'ath and suspecting Mu'awiya's political involvement.

Olympe de Gouges

Birth date: May 6, 1748

Death date: November 2, 1793

Age: 45

Olympe de Gouges, born Marie Gouze, was a French playwright, political activist, abolitionist, and pioneering advocate for women’s rights. She is best remembered for her 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, a bold response to the male-centered ideals of the French Revolution. Associated with moderate Girondin politics and increasingly critical of revolutionary extremism, she was arrested during the Reign of Terror and executed by guillotine in Paris on 3 November 1793 at the age of 45.

Evangelista Torricelli

Birth date: October 14, 1608

Death date: October 24, 1647

Age: 39

Evangelista Torricelli was an Italian physicist and mathematician, remembered above all for inventing the mercury barometer and for work that helped clarify air pressure, motion, optics, and early ideas related to calculus. A pupil of Benedetto Castelli and later connected with Galileo’s circle in Florence, he became one of the sharpest scientific minds of seventeenth-century Italy. His career was brief: in October 1647 he died in Florence after a fever, most likely typhoid, only ten days after turning 39.

Eva Perón

Birth date: May 6, 1919

Death date: July 25, 1952

Age: 33

Eva Perón, widely known as Evita, was an Argentine actress, political leader, and First Lady of Argentina from 1946 to 1952 as the wife of President Juan Perón. She became a central figure of Peronism, championed labor rights and women's suffrage, founded the Female Peronist Party, and led the Eva Perón Foundation, which made her beloved among many working-class Argentines. In 1951, declining health and opposition from powerful institutions forced her to abandon a bid for the vice presidency. She died of cancer in Buenos Aires on 1952-07-26 at the age of 33 and received a state funeral.

Robert Falcon Scott

Birth date: June 5, 1868

Death date: March 28, 1912

Age: 43

Robert Falcon Scott was a British Royal Navy officer and Antarctic explorer who led the Discovery expedition and later the Terra Nova expedition, becoming one of the best-known figures of the heroic age of polar exploration. His party reached the South Pole in January 1912, only to find that Roald Amundsen had arrived first. Exhausted, starving, and trapped by extreme Antarctic weather on the return journey, Scott and his last companions died in their tent in late March 1912.

Thomas Sankara

Birth date: December 20, 1949

Death date: October 14, 1987

Age: 37

Thomas Sankara was a Burkinabé military officer, Pan-Africanist revolutionary, and president of Burkina Faso from 1983 to 1987. He became known for anti-corruption measures, mass vaccination drives, literacy efforts, reforestation, women’s rights reforms, and renaming Upper Volta as Burkina Faso. His bold socialist and anti-imperialist agenda made him an enduring symbol of African self-reliance. On 15 October 1987, he was assassinated in Ouagadougou during a coup linked to his former ally Blaise Compaoré.

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec

Birth date: November 23, 1864

Death date: September 8, 1901

Age: 36

Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was a French painter, printmaker, draughtsman, caricaturist, and illustrator whose sharp, vivid scenes of Parisian nightlife made him one of the defining artists of fin-de-siècle Montmartre. Born into an aristocratic family, he became closely associated with cabarets, performers, cafés, and brothels, creating iconic images of the Moulin Rouge and the bohemian world around it. His health declined severely in his final years, worsened by alcoholism and syphilis; after strokes and paralysis, he died at his mother's estate, Château Malromé, on 9 September 1901, aged 36.

Death date: December 8, 1641

Sir Anthony van Dyck was a Flemish Baroque painter whose elegant portraits transformed European court portraiture, especially through his work for Charles I of England and the English aristocracy. He died in London after returning there ill in late 1641, and his burial in St Paul’s Cathedral reflected the extraordinary status he had achieved by the age of 42.

Nat King Cole

Death date: February 14, 1965

Age: 45

Nat King Cole was an American singer, jazz pianist, and actor whose warm baritone voice and elegant piano style made him one of the defining entertainers of the mid-20th century. He rose from the King Cole Trio to international solo fame with classics such as "Unforgettable," "Mona Lisa," and "The Christmas Song," while also breaking television barriers as the host of a nationally broadcast variety show. He died in Santa Monica on February 15, 1965, at age 45, after being diagnosed with lung cancer.

Nestor Makhno

Birth date: November 6, 1888

Death date: July 24, 1934

Age: 45

Nestor Makhno was a Ukrainian anarchist revolutionary, peasant organizer, and commander of the Revolutionary Insurgent Army of Ukraine during the upheavals of the Russian Civil War and Ukrainian War of Independence. Known as Bat'ko Makhno, he became the emblematic leader of the Makhnovshchina, a radical movement that sought free soviets, land redistribution, and anarchist communism in southern Ukraine. After defeat by the Bolsheviks, he lived in exile in Europe and settled in Paris, where poverty, wounds, malnutrition, and tuberculosis weakened him. He died there on 25 July 1934 at the age of 45.

Pancho Villa

Death date: July 19, 1923

Age: 45

Pancho Villa, born José Doroteo Arango Arámbula, was one of the most charismatic commanders of the Mexican Revolution, leading the División del Norte and becoming a symbol of northern Mexico’s revolutionary energy. He helped overthrow the old Porfirian order, served as provisional governor of Chihuahua, and became famous internationally through journalism, corridos, and film. After retiring under an amnesty, he was ambushed and assassinated in Parral, Chihuahua, on 20 July 1923.

Sylvia Plath

Birth date: October 26, 1932

Death date: February 10, 1963

Age: 30

Sylvia Plath was an American poet, novelist, and short-story writer whose intense, sharply crafted work helped define confessional poetry. She is best remembered for The Bell Jar, The Colossus, Ariel, and the posthumously Pulitzer-winning Collected Poems. Plath’s writing turned personal anguish into disciplined art, exploring identity, ambition, motherhood, alienation, and self-destruction with rare force. She died by suicide in London on February 11, 1963, during a severe depressive period, at the age of 30.

Jean-François Champollion

Birth date: December 22, 1790

Death date: March 3, 1832

Age: 41

Jean-François Champollion was a French philologist and orientalist best known for deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs, a breakthrough that opened ancient Egyptian texts to modern scholarship and made him a founding figure of Egyptology. A gifted linguist from youth, he used Coptic, Greek, and the Rosetta Stone to show that hieroglyphs combined phonetic and ideographic signs. After a demanding scholarly career and an expedition to Egypt, his health deteriorated; he died in Paris on 4 March 1832, reportedly after an apoplectic attack, at the age of 41.

Why this is controversial: Martin Bormann was a senior Nazi Party official, Adolf Hitler's private secretary, and head of the Nazi Party Chancellery. He helped administer and enforce Nazi rule, influenced policy and appointments, and was convicted in absentia at Nuremberg for war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Martin Ludwig Bormann was a German Nazi Party official who became one of Adolf Hitler’s most powerful aides, serving as head of the Nazi Party Chancellery and Hitler’s private secretary. He controlled access to Hitler, influenced appointments and legislation, and was later convicted in absentia at the Nuremberg trials for war crimes and crimes against humanity. As Soviet forces closed in on Berlin, Bormann fled the Führerbunker on 2 May 1945 and most likely died by suicide near Lehrter station; his remains were found decades later and confirmed as his.

Marvin Gaye was an American soul, R&B, and Motown singer-songwriter whose expressive voice and ambitious albums helped redefine popular music in the 1960s and 1970s. Death date: December 27, 1925

Age: 30

Sergei Yesenin was one of the most beloved Russian lyric poets of the early 20th century, celebrated for musical, emotionally direct poems rooted in village life, nature, love, rebellion, and the cultural upheavals around the Russian Revolution. Associated with the Imaginist movement, he became famous young and lived intensely, with turbulent relationships and public notoriety. He died in Leningrad in December 1925, officially by suicide in a hotel room after writing a final farewell poem; later theories questioned the circumstances, but suicide remains the standard account.

Chadwick Boseman

Birth date: November 28, 1976

Death date: August 27, 2020

Age: 43

Chadwick Aaron Boseman was an American actor and playwright whose calm intensity and sense of purpose made him one of the defining screen figures of his generation. After studying directing at Howard University, he broke through portraying Jackie Robinson in 42, then played James Brown in Get on Up and Thurgood Marshall in Marshall. He became internationally famous as T’Challa, the Black Panther, in the Marvel Cinematic Universe, bringing dignity, charisma, and cultural weight to a landmark superhero role. Boseman died in Los Angeles on August 28, 2020, at age 43, after a private four-year battle with colon cancer that he had kept from the public while continuing to work.

Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz

Birth date: November 11, 1648

Death date: April 16, 1695

Age: 46

Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a brilliant nun, poet, dramatist, philosopher, and scholar of colonial New Spain, celebrated as one of the great voices of the Spanish Baroque and an early defender of women’s intellectual freedom. She wrote poetry, plays, theological prose, and sharp arguments for women’s education while living in a convent in Mexico City. In her final years she faced pressure from church authorities and appears to have withdrawn from public literary life. She died in Mexico City on 17 April 1695, aged 46, after caring for fellow nuns during a plague outbreak.

Age: 43

Carl Wilhelm Scheele was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist whose experimental skill made him one of the most productive chemical discoverers of the eighteenth century. He independently discovered oxygen before Joseph Priestley published, identified chlorine, and helped reveal substances connected with molybdenum, tungsten, barium, manganese, and many organic and inorganic acids. He worked mainly as a pharmacist rather than as a university professor, which partly explains why his fame lagged behind his achievements. Scheele died in Köping on 21 May 1786 at the age of 43, after years of dangerous laboratory exposure; contemporary and later accounts often connect his decline with poisoning from toxic substances such as mercury, arsenic, lead compounds, cyanides, and acids.

He confessed to 30 murders, though the true number of victims remains uncertain. After convictions for murders in Florida, he received multiple death sentences and was executed in the electric chair at Florida State Prison on January 24, 1989, at age 42.

Georges Jacques Danton was one of the most powerful voices of the French Revolution: a lawyer, electrifying orator, Cordeliers Club figure, minister of justice, and early member of the Committee of Public Safety. Accused of corruption, conspiracy, and political betrayal by his enemies, he was tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal and guillotined in Paris on 5 April 1794 at the age of 34.

Charles V of France, known as Charles the Wise, ruled from 1364 to 1380 and became one of the most effective Valois kings during the Hundred Years’ War. With careful taxation, diplomacy, fortified cities, a reorganized army, and commanders such as Bertrand du Guesclin, he recovered much of the territory lost to England and strengthened royal government. In his final years he suffered from a long-standing abscess or fistula; when it dried up in September 1380, he prepared for death, tried to abolish the unpopular hearth tax, and died at 42, leaving the throne to his young son Charles VI.

Amedeo Modigliani

Birth date: July 11, 1884

Death date: January 23, 1920

Age: 35

Amedeo Modigliani was an Italian painter and sculptor associated with the École de Paris, best known for elegant portraits and nudes with elongated faces, necks, and figures. Born in Livorno, he moved to Paris in 1906 and became part of the avant-garde world around Montparnasse, developing a style that was little rewarded during his lifetime but later became iconic. His health, long weakened by tuberculosis and hard living, collapsed in January 1920; he died in Paris of tubercular meningitis at the age of 35.

Henry V of England

Birth date: September 15, 1386

Death date: August 30, 1422

Age: 35

Henry V of England, also known as Henry of Monmouth, was a Lancastrian king whose short reign became famous for military ambition, royal discipline, and the dramatic English victory at Agincourt during the Hundred Years' War. He forced the Treaty of Troyes, making himself heir to the French throne. He died at 35 at Vincennes near Paris, most likely from dysentery contracted during campaigning after the Siege of Meaux, before he could inherit France.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer

Birth date: February 3, 1906

Death date: April 8, 1945

Age: 39

Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a German Lutheran pastor, theologian, and anti-Nazi dissident, known for his role in the Confessing Church and for influential works such as The Cost of Discipleship. He opposed Nazi control of the churches and became connected with resistance circles around the Abwehr. Arrested by the Gestapo in 1943, he was later accused of links to the anti-Hitler conspiracy and hanged at Flossenbürg concentration camp on 9 April 1945, just weeks before Germany’s surrender.

Julian

Death date: June 25, 363

Age: 31

Julian, known as Julian the Apostate, was a Roman emperor, scholar, military commander, and philosopher who ruled from 361 to 363. A nephew of Constantine the Great, he was raised in the imperial family, governed Gaul successfully, and tried to revive traditional Roman religion after rejecting Christianity. In 363, during his Persian campaign, he was mortally wounded near Samarra while retreating from Mesopotamia and died shortly afterward at the age of 31.

Extremely controversial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Reinhard Heydrich is one of the most notorious figures of Nazi Germany. He was a senior SS and security official, led major organs of Nazi terror, chaired the Wannsee Conference, and was one of the principal organizers of the Holocaust.

Reinhard Heydrich was a high-ranking SS and police official in Nazi Germany and one of the principal architects of the Holocaust. As head of the Reich Security Main Office, he oversaw major instruments of Nazi terror, including the Gestapo, Kripo, and SD, and chaired the 1942 Wannsee Conference, where plans for the genocide of Europe’s Jews were coordinated. He was mortally wounded in Prague during Operation Anthropoid, an assassination carried out by Czechoslovak agents, and died of sepsis from his injuries on 4 June 1942 at the age of 38.

Lucrezia Borgia was an Italian Renaissance noblewoman of the powerful Borgia family, daughter of Pope Alexander VI and Vannozza dei Cattanei. Her marriages to Giovanni Sforza, Alfonso of Aragon, and Alfonso I d'Este made her a political figure in Rome, Naples, and Ferrara, while later legend turned her into one of the most controversial women of Renaissance history. Spartacus

Birth date: December 31, 103 BCE

Death date: March 31, 71 BCE

Age: 32

Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who became the most famous leader of the Third Servile War, the major slave uprising against the Roman Republic from 73 to 71 BC. After escaping a gladiatorial school near Capua, he helped turn a small band of fugitives into a powerful rebel force that defeated several Roman armies. His life is known mostly from later writers such as Plutarch and Appian, and he became an enduring symbol of resistance against oppression. In 71 BC, his army was finally defeated by forces under Marcus Licinius Crassus; Spartacus is believed to have been killed in the final battle, though his body was never identified.

Edward IV of England

Birth date: April 27, 1442

Death date: April 8, 1483

Age: 40

Edward IV was the first Yorkist king of England and one of the central rulers of the Wars of the Roses. He seized the throne from Henry VI in 1461, lost it briefly in 1470, and regained it after decisive victories at Barnet and Tewkesbury in 1471. His later reign was comparatively stable, though shaped by dynastic tension and the political consequences of his marriage to Elizabeth Woodville. He fell seriously ill around Easter 1483 and died at Westminster on 9 April 1483, aged 40; his young son Edward V succeeded him but was soon displaced by Richard III.

Janis Joplin was an American singer and songwriter whose raw, powerful voice made her one of the defining performers of 1960s rock and blues. She rose to fame with Big Brother and the Holding Company, stunned audiences at Monterey Pop, later played Woodstock, and left classics such as "Piece of My Heart" and "Me and Bobby McGee." In October 1970, while still at the height of her fame and working on the album Pearl, she died in Los Angeles from a heroin overdose at the age of 27.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Ismail I is highly controversial because he founded the Safavid state through military conquest and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, a transformation associated with coercion, sectarian conflict, and long-lasting religious-political consequences. He is also an important state-builder and cultural patron, but his legacy is inseparable from violence, forced religious change, and imperial warfare.

Ismail I, also known as Shah Ismail I, was the founder of the Safavid dynasty and the first shah of Safavid Iran, ruling from 1501 to 1524. He unified much of Iran, made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, and became an important patron and poet under the pen name Khatai. His later reign was overshadowed by the Ottoman victory at Chaldiran in 1514, after which he withdrew from active campaigning. He died on 23 May 1524 at the age of 36 and was buried at Ardabil.

Death date: December 31, 1324 BCE

Age: 19

Tutankhamun, often called King Tut, was a pharaoh of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty who came to the throne as a child and helped restore the traditional religion after the Amarna period. His own reign was brief, but his fame became global after Howard Carter discovered his remarkably rich tomb in 1922. He died young at about 19, probably after a combination of illness and physical injury, and his unexpected death helps explain why he was buried in a relatively small tomb that still transformed modern understanding of ancient Egypt.

Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky was a Soviet psychologist whose ideas reshaped developmental and educational psychology, especially through the zone of proximal development, inner speech, and the social formation of mind. He died in Moscow from tuberculosis in June 1934, still only 37, leaving a compact but unusually powerful body of work.

Sándor Petőfi was a Hungarian poet, journalist and revolutionary, widely regarded as Hungary's national poet and one of the defining voices of the 1848 Revolution. He disappeared during the Battle of Segesvár on 31 July 1849 while serving with the revolutionary forces; he is generally believed to have been killed there, although his body was never conclusively identified.

Romy Schneider, born Rosemarie Magdalena Albach in Vienna, was one of European cinema’s defining actresses, rising to fame as Empress Elisabeth in the beloved Sissi films before reinventing herself in France through deeper, more modern roles with directors such as Luchino Visconti, Claude Sautet, and Jacques Deray. Her later life was marked by private grief, especially the accidental death of her son David in 1981. Peter III of Russia

Death date: July 16, 1762

Age: 34

Peter III of Russia, born Karl Peter Ulrich of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorp, was the grandson of Peter the Great and briefly ruled as Emperor of Russia in 1762. Raised between German and Russian dynastic worlds, he inherited Holstein-Gottorp and was chosen as heir by Empress Elizabeth. His short reign brought reforms, but his admiration for Prussia and reversal of Russian gains in the Seven Years’ War made him deeply unpopular among powerful elites. After only about six months on the throne, he was overthrown in a palace coup led by supporters of his wife, Catherine II. He was taken to Ropsha and died soon afterward under murky circumstances, officially explained as illness but widely suspected to have involved violence.

Age: 36

Vissarion Grigoryevich Belinsky was one of the defining Russian literary critics of the 1830s and 1840s, a Westernizer whose essays helped shape the careers of major writers and the tone of Russia’s emerging radical intelligentsia. He championed reason, social responsibility, and individual rights in literature and public life. Belinsky died in Saint Petersburg on 7 June 1848, aged 36, after suffering from consumption, now understood as tuberculosis, shortly before the authorities could arrest him for his political views.

Birth date: October 1, 1452

Death date: August 21, 1485

Age: 32
Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Richard III remains one of England’s most disputed monarchs. His seizure of the throne after the young Edward V and his brother were declared illegitimate, the unresolved disappearance of the Princes in the Tower, and later Tudor and Shakespearean portrayals made him a lasting symbol of suspected usurpation and political murder, even though modern historians debate how much blame is justified.

Richard III of England was the last king of the House of York and the final Plantagenet monarch, ruling from 1483 to 1485 during the turbulent Wars of the Roses. Brother of Edward IV, he became king after the young Edward V and his brother were declared illegitimate, a controversy tied forever to the mystery of the Princes in the Tower. Richard died aged 32 at the Battle of Bosworth Field, where Henry Tudor defeated him and founded the Tudor dynasty as Henry VII.

Heinrich von Kleist was a German poet, dramatist, novelist, short-story writer, and journalist whose intense, psychologically charged works include The Broken Jug, Penthesilea, The Prince of Homburg, Michael Kohlhaas, and The Marquise of O. Honorius, born Flavius Honorius, was Western Roman emperor during one of the empire’s most unstable periods. Dylan Marlais Thomas was a Welsh poet, writer, and broadcaster whose musical, image-rich language made him one of the most distinctive literary voices of the 20th century. During his final American tour in 1953, Thomas became seriously ill in New York, fell into a coma, and died on 9 November 1953 at the age of 39; later accounts have emphasized pneumonia and severe respiratory illness, while also noting the long-running myths around alcohol and medical treatment.

Charles XII of Sweden, also known as Karl XII or Carolus Rex, was the Swedish king from 1697 to 1718 and one of the most famous warrior-monarchs of the Great Northern War. Lucius Verus was a Roman emperor of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty, ruling from 161 to 169 alongside his adoptive brother Marcus Aurelius. Louis VIII of France, nicknamed the Lion, was a Capetian king who ruled from 1223 to 1226 after years as a forceful prince. He campaigned in England during the First Barons' War, pressed French claims against the Angevin Empire, and expanded royal authority in Poitou, Saintonge, La Rochelle, and Languedoc. His reign was brief but energetic. While returning north from the Albigensian Crusade, he fell ill with dysentery and died at Château de Montpensier on 8 November 1226, aged 39.

Commodus was a Roman emperor, the son of Marcus Aurelius, who ruled first as co-emperor and then alone from 180 to 192. His reign is often remembered as a turning point after the stability of the Pax Romana, marked by court intrigue, autocratic rule, and his notorious public performances as a gladiator. In late 192, after a conspiracy formed around members of his inner circle, he was first poisoned unsuccessfully and then strangled by the wrestler Narcissus, dying in Rome at the age of 31.

His reign is remembered for the Antonine Constitution, which extended Roman citizenship to most free inhabitants of the empire, and for the monumental Baths of Caracalla in Rome. In 217, while campaigning in the East against Parthia, he was assassinated near Carrhae by a soldier, Justin Martialis, in a plot associated with the future emperor Macrinus.

After being discovered guarding barrels of gunpowder beneath Parliament, he was tortured, tried for high treason, and sentenced to be hanged, drawn and quartered. Enver Pasha was an Ottoman Turkish military officer, revolutionary, and leading member of the Committee of Union and Progress. A central figure of the Young Turk movement, he became minister of war and one of the powerful Three Pashas who dominated the Ottoman Empire during World War I. Death date: March 31, 1922

Age: 34

Charles I of Austria, also Charles IV of Hungary, was the last Habsburg ruler of Austria-Hungary, reigning from 1916 until the monarchy collapsed at the end of the First World War. He tried to preserve the empire and sought a negotiated peace, but exile followed the postwar republican settlements. After failed attempts to regain the Hungarian throne, he was sent to Madeira, where a cold developed into bronchitis and pneumonia. He died there of respiratory failure on 1 April 1922, aged 34.

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola was an Italian Renaissance nobleman and philosopher, celebrated for his astonishing learning, his 900 Theses, and the Oration on the Dignity of Man, a landmark text of Renaissance humanism. Lucan, born Marcus Annaeus Lucanus in Corduba in AD 39, was a brilliant Roman poet of Nero’s age and the author of the unfinished epic Pharsalia, a fierce retelling of the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey that made him one of the standout voices of Imperial Latin literature. Ibrahim I was the Ottoman sultan from 1640 to 1648, the son of Ahmed I and Kösem Sultan, and a ruler whose reign became associated with palace factionalism, financial strain, war pressure, and stories of unstable behavior. Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Blackbeard is highly controversial because he was a pirate whose fame rests on maritime robbery, intimidation, hostage-taking, and violence. Later popular culture often romanticizes him, but his historical reputation is tied to criminal raiding and fear.

Blackbeard, born Edward Teach or Thatch, was an English pirate whose short but spectacular career made him the model of the terrifying sea raider. Operating in the West Indies and along the North American coast, he captured La Concorde, renamed it Queen Anne's Revenge, and built his reputation through intimidation, theatrical menace, and daring attacks such as the blockade of Charles Town. After accepting a pardon and returning to piracy, he was cornered near Ocracoke by a force led by Lieutenant Robert Maynard. On 22 November 1718, Blackbeard was killed in a violent boarding fight, reportedly suffering multiple gunshot and blade wounds before being beheaded.

Katherine Mansfield, born Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp in Wellington, New Zealand, was one of the defining short-story writers of literary modernism. She built a lasting reputation in England and Europe and was connected to major modernist circles around writers such as Virginia Woolf and D. H. Lawrence. Mansfield’s health collapsed after she developed tuberculosis, diagnosed in 1917. She spent her final years moving through Europe in search of relief and unconventional treatments, and died in France near Fontainebleau on 9 January 1923 at the age of 34.

Elagabalus was a teenage Roman emperor of the Severan dynasty who ruled from 218 to 222 CE after rising from his role as priest of the sun god Elagabal in Emesa. His reign became famous for religious upheaval, court scandal, and conflict with Rome’s political elite; in March 222 he was assassinated by the Praetorian Guard during a coup and replaced by Severus Alexander.

Controverial historical figure

Why this is controversial: Charlotte Corday is highly controversial because she assassinated Jean-Paul Marat during the French Revolution. She has been interpreted both as a political murderer and as a figure who believed she was acting against revolutionary violence, making her legacy sharply divided.

Charlotte Corday was a French political figure of the Revolution, born into minor Norman nobility and known for her support of the Girondins against the radical Jacobins. She entered history in July 1793 when she travelled to Paris and fatally stabbed Jean-Paul Marat in his bath, believing his influence was driving France deeper into violence. Arrested immediately, she was tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal and guillotined four days later at the age of 24.

His legacy depends strongly on whether he is viewed through anti-imperial resistance, revolutionary socialism, or opposition to violent tactics.

Bhagat Singh was an Indian anti-colonial revolutionary whose writings, activism, and role in the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association made him one of the best-known figures of the independence movement. Arrested after the Central Legislative Assembly bombing and linked to the Saunders case, he was executed by hanging in Lahore in 1931 at age 23, becoming a lasting symbol of resistance.

Grand Duchess Maria Nikolaevna of Russia

Birth date: June 25, 1899

Death date: July 16, 1918

Age: 19

Grand Duchess Maria Nikolaevna of Russia was the third daughter of Tsar Nicholas II and Empress Alexandra Feodorovna, remembered for her warm nature, close bond with her siblings, and visits to wounded soldiers during World War I. After the Romanovs were imprisoned following the Russian Revolution, she was executed with her parents, brother, sisters, and loyal attendants at the Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg on 17 July 1918.

Carlo Acutis

Birth date: May 2, 1991

Death date: October 11, 2006

Age: 15

Carlo Acutis was an English-born Italian Catholic teenager, computer enthusiast, and creator of a widely shared website documenting Eucharistic miracles, which made him an enduring symbol of youthful faith in the digital age. Raised in Milan and canonized in 2025 as the first millennial saint of the Catholic Church, he died in Monza in 2006 after a short illness caused by acute promyelocytic leukemia, at the age of 15.

Carloman II of France

Birth date: December 31, 866

Death date: December 5, 884

Age: 18

Carloman II of West Francia was a young Carolingian king who inherited the western Frankish realm with his brother Louis III in 879 and ruled alone from 882, trying to hold together a kingdom strained by Viking attacks and powerful nobles. He died near Les Andelys in December 884 after a hunting accident, when a servant accidentally speared his leg during a wild-boar encounter, ending his reign at about 18.
