Herennius Etruscus

Birth date: December 31, 227

Death date: June 14, 251

Age: 24

Herennius Etruscus was the elder son of Emperor Decius and a Roman co-emperor in 251, raised from Caesar to Augustus during the empire's third-century crisis while campaigning on the Danube against the Goths. His reign lasted only weeks before he was killed at the Battle of Abritus, probably in June 251, when the Roman army fell into a disastrous Gothic ambush and his father died in the same campaign.

Alexandros IV of Macedon

Birth date: July 31, 323 BCE

Death date: August 30, 309 BCE

Age: 14

Alexander IV of Macedon was the posthumous son of Alexander the Great and Roxana, proclaimed king while still an infant and carried through the violent wars of the Successors as the last legitimate heir of the Argead dynasty. He never exercised real power, and when he was nearing the age to rule for himself, Cassander had the teenage king and his mother secretly murdered, ending Alexander the Great’s direct legitimate line.

Louis II of Hungary

Birth date: June 30, 1506

Death date: August 28, 1526

Age: 20

Louis II of Hungary was the young Jagiellonian ruler of Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia from 1516 until 1526, remembered as the last king to rule all of medieval Hungary before the Ottoman breakthrough. Crowned as a child and thrust into a fragile kingdom under growing pressure from Sultan Suleiman, he became one of the tragic symbols of Central Europe’s turning point. He died at just 20 after the Battle of Mohács, when the Hungarian army was crushed by the Ottomans and the king was killed while fleeing the battlefield, a catastrophe that opened the way to the partition of Hungary.

Władysław III of Poland

Birth date: October 30, 1424

Death date: November 9, 1444

Age: 20

Władysław III of Poland, also known as Ladislaus of Varna, was king of Poland from 1434 and king of Hungary and Croatia from 1440, a young Jagiellon ruler drawn into the struggle against Ottoman expansion. After early successes in the Crusade of Varna, he died in the Battle of Varna in 1444 during a charge against the Ottoman forces, and his body was never definitively recovered.

Leo II

Birth date: December 31, 467

Death date: November 9, 474

Age: 7

Leo II was the child emperor of the Eastern Roman Empire in 474, grandson of Leo I and son of Zeno, raised to the throne to secure the dynasty during a tense political moment in Constantinople. After only a few months as emperor and co-ruler with his father, he died in the capital at about age 7 in late 474, most likely of natural causes, though later writers sometimes suspected poisoning because his death left Zeno as sole ruler.

Cameron Boyce

Birth date: May 27, 1999

Death date: July 5, 2019

Age: 20

American actor who rose to fame as a child star and became widely known for Disney Channel's Jessie, the Descendants films, and roles in Grown Ups and Eagle Eye. He died in Los Angeles at age 20 after an epileptic seizure; the medical examiner ruled it sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, just weeks before Descendants 3 premiered.

Faisal II of Iraq

Birth date: May 1, 1935

Death date: July 13, 1958

Age: 23

Faisal II was the last King of Iraq, born in Baghdad in 1935 and placed on the throne as a child after the death of his father, King Ghazi. His reign ended during the 14 July Revolution in 1958, when he was killed at al-Rihab Palace in Baghdad, bringing the Hashemite monarchy in Iraq to an abrupt end.

Did you know:

For most of history, a drink of water was also a gamble. Rivers, wells, and town pumps could carry sewage-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. In the United States, typhoid fever was about 100 cases per 100,000 people in 1900; after water treatment, sanitation, and disinfection spread, it fell to 33.8 by 1920 and 0.1 by 2006. A glass of boring tap water may be one of the greatest inventions in history.

The humbling part is that this is not ancient history everywhere. WHO estimates that around 1 million people still die each year from diarrhoea linked to unsafe drinking water, sanitation, and hand hygiene. So when someone in a modern city turns a tap, showers, brushes teeth, and flushes a toilet without thinking, they are living inside a public-health miracle.
